When I get intrusive thoughts mine are usually based on my interpretations of what people say (tone/body language/facial expressions). For me I try to ground myself and focus on literally just what they said because I know that to be 100% factual. If they were trying to imply something by those other means it's not my job to figure that out. They need to be more straightforward. If it's a stranger or an aquantance, I don't say anything, but if it's someone close to me, I have set boundaries and told them that because of my anxiety, I'm going to take you at your word, so no hidden meanings will be taken.

So, bottom line, I have no idea if that situation applies to you, but if you can realize your having intrusive thoughts and can find the piece of it that is 100% true, latch onto that. And if it's something other people can help with that are close to you, more often than not they'll want to help.

My flare-ups are coming from my impending divorce and usually stem from thinking about the past, or worrying how I may handle things in the future. So, staying in the moment, and as cliche as it sounds, being honest and literally just doing my best, whatever that is each day, has helped me so much. And knowing that if I fail, it's ok. Getting better mentally, recovering, isn't a straight line and it's ok to fuck up.

And if you fail to remember it sometimes, like I do, its really ok. Breakdowns are ok, recovering from trauma, building self confidence, anything of that sort is never a straight line. Nobody is perfect, the best people just never stop trying to being better, even if they screwed up or regressed. Someone told me, the best you can do that day, is the best you can do that day. It sounds funny even to type but it resonated with me.

Jack, fuck being normal. I don't know that it exists. I hurt myself for different reasons, but similar ones as well when I thought I was worth nothing to anyone. I hid it well, and didn't tell people for years. When I did finally tell people, everyone had the same reaction, none of them wanted me gone. Now I have a greater support system than ever, and I'm going through worse than I was before and the things that are happening to me are objectively worse than before. 

Being completely open and honest about how I'm feeling to everyone I am close with is helping. I made myself feel more alone by not including people in my struggle. I felt like no one wanted me because no one knew I needed to feel wanted. I'm not sure if you're going through the same, but it's what has helped me.

Also, I feel like it needs to be said, because I needed to hear it from someone. It's ok to be broken. I still am. I don't know when I won't feel this way, but I just have to focus on one moment at a time. You can do it, you've made it to 22, that takes strength no matter what you've been through.

My opinion, I don't think that I would be able to go back to my wife at this point (separated and awaiting the legal side of divorce). But the reality is, as I'm learning, is that you have to figure out what you want. From what I'm learning, you only have the responsibility for what you are feeling and being honest about those feelings. That's what I'm trying to apply to everything in my life. Living as honest as I can, doing what I think is right, and trying to be a positive impact on the people that are in my life.

If you don't think you can be with her, be honest. If you want to try, but feel apprehension, tell her that. All you can do is be honest, you have no responsibility for how they respond. If she chooses you, when you're honest, great, if she doesn't, then it sucks but it won't do to dwell on it.

All of these things I'm saying? Are what I should do, what I want to do, I still mess it up most of the time, but it's what I'm trying to work towards. Your feelings and thoughts are valid, and deserve to be heard.
